extracted.intended_audience: practicing geometers and mathematical problem-solvers (readers of The Mathematician; advanced undergraduates and professional mathematicians interested in classical geometry, analytical geometry and mechanics problems)
extracted.subtask_description: Providing worked solutions and methodological guidance for classical geometry, conic-section, analytic-geometry and mechanics problems; includes multiple independent solution methods, cautions about algebraic methods, and use of tangency/degeneracy arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose convenient coordinate axes
rubrics_metrics.description: Take A as the origin, AB as the axis of x and AC as that of y.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set up coordinate systems to simplify the coordinates of given points and the algebraic form of curves (e.g., place a vertex or side on an axis, choose origin at a triangle vertex or circle centre). Several solutions begin by fixing axes to make subsequent algebra straightforward.

rubrics_metrics.name: Find invariant ratios independent of auxiliary distances
rubrics_metrics.description: These ratios, it is to be observed, are independent of di and d^*.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When parameters (like distances from midpoints) appear, seek combinations or ratios of coefficients that do not depend on those auxiliary parameters — invariants that show the result holds for any choice of those distances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpret parameter ranges to determine geometric location
rubrics_metrics.description: When they are less than the halves of the respective sides, the points are in the sides; when greater, in the sides produced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always check the size/sign of parameters to tell whether constructed points lie on a segment or its extension — this affects case distinctions and validity of constructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exploit symmetry and principal axes
rubrics_metrics.description: By symmetry; .:. A = B = JC. (For the circle the principal moments are equal.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use symmetry to reduce the number of distinct quantities (e.g., equal moments/invariants), simplifying calculations and allowing immediate identifications of coefficients or moments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduce dimensionality by projection
rubrics_metrics.description: The given circle be projected on a plane perpendicular to the axis … The projection will be an ellipse of which the axis major is 2a, and the axis minor 2a sin a. The moment of inertia of the ellipse is the same as that of the circle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Project 3D geometry problems onto an appropriate plane to produce a simpler 2D figure (e.g., project a rotating circle to an ellipse) that preserves the quantity of interest (like moment of inertia), then compute on the simpler figure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide multiple independent solutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiple solutions are given (First Solution, Second Solution, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Offer alternative methods (analytic, geometric, mechanical, projection, virtual work) to both check results and provide different insights; the periodical frequently presents several independent approaches to the same problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply mechanics or virtual-works where appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: The problem may also be solved by virtual velocities. … For the equilibrium … the tangential components of the weights must be equal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For equilibrium or physical-interpretation problems (e.g., weights on a string over a curve), apply principles from mechanics (force resolution, virtual work, equilibrium of tangential components) as a legitimate method of solution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substitute coordinates into a general conic equation to determine coefficients
rubrics_metrics.description: Assume the equation to a conic section passing through the first five points. From (1) and the first four of the preceding co-ordinates we obtain … From these equations we readily find D = — Ac and E = — BJ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the general second-degree equation, substitute known point coordinates, and solve the linear system for coefficients (or their ratios). This algebraic approach is standard for proving concyclicity or that points lie on the same conic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Check limiting and special cases (corollaries)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the sides of the triangle are indefinitely diminished it becomes a point; hence if in a plane three straight lines passing through a point are bisected in that point, their extremities are in the same conic section. … From (4), when a = 0, or a = 90°, we have the moments as expressed in (2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Validate results by examining special or limiting values of parameters (degenerate cases, right-angle cases, zero-angle) to ensure formulas reduce to known or simpler results and to derive corollaries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exploit interchange/symmetry of coordinates to deduce extra points/relations
rubrics_metrics.description: The latter system may be deduced from the former by interchanging X and y… But by such an interchanging the equation (1) remains unaltered, since u and v merely interchange. Hence whether we seek to determine k from the 1st or 2nd systems … the same result; and therefore if the curve (1) be made to pass through V it will also pass through T.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a formula is symmetric under interchange of variables, use that symmetry to obtain additional points or relations without new computation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use tangent planes/enveloping cones and tangency conditions to determine coefficients
rubrics_metrics.description: The equations of tangent planes at the points specified above, are … As these all pass through the same point, and as three planes are sufficient to determine a point, these equations are equivalent to three independent equations which will express a, β, γ in terms of the co-ordinates of the five points, and α, β, γ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For surfaces of second degree sharing points, include tangent-plane (contact) conditions: common tangents/enveloping cones give additional independent equations to determine otherwise undetermined coefficients.

rubrics_metrics.name: Count conditions / degrees of freedom to know how many points/tangents suffice
rubrics_metrics.description: If any one of the first six coefficients … be arbitrary and independent of the eight remaining coefficients, these eight coefficients will be functions of the co-ordinates of the eight points through which all the surfaces thus represented pass.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use parameter counting — number of independent coefficients versus number of conditions (points, tangent planes, infinitely near points) — to judge how many constraints are required to determine a conic/surface uniquely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combine equations to get line through intersections
rubrics_metrics.description: Uz + kti^ = is the equation to a line through the intersection of ti2 and 2^3. … Now combining … we obtain … which … represents the diagonal of the hexagon joining … and consequently the lines joining the intersections … intersect in the same point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Form linear combinations of two plane/line equations to obtain the equation of the line through their intersection; combining relations is a standard analytic-geometry technique to exhibit concurrency or collinearity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use classical theorems (Brianchon, Pascal, Monge) to simplify geometric arguments
rubrics_metrics.description: Since the sides of the hexagon touch the conic section, its diagonals MP, QN, and CF intersect in the same point (by Brianchon's theorem) … By Pascal's theorem …
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reference and apply established theorems from projective/conic geometry to avoid reinventing longer proofs and to connect your construction to known, powerful results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious with the method of arbitrary coefficients — avoid false generality
rubrics_metrics.description: If in any inquiry having reference to surfaces that have eight points common, we can shew by the method of arbitrary coefficients, that a property holds in each case, that is, when each coefficient is arbitrary, all we prove is that it is true for some particular positions of the eight points. It is indeed very probable, that a property thus investigated, is generally true ; but a safer mode of demonstration in such cases is by an arbitrary multiplier (see p. 12). It will be obvious that if a theorem fail by this method for any one coefficient, it must fail in general.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume that demonstrating a property under an assumption 'make coefficient X arbitrary' proves the general case; prefer using an arbitrary multiplier (linear combination) to prove generality. If a property fails under one arbitrary-coefficient specialization, it fails in general.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not equate algebraic factors to zero unless dependence justifies it
rubrics_metrics.description: We should not be justified in equating to zero each factor of that result as I have done. This we could do only when each factor is indeterminate in the ordinary sense, that is, when each factor involves variables that are functions of each other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When an equation factorizes, do not set individual factors to zero unless you have established that those factors are dependent (indeterminate) in the context; otherwise equating each to zero can produce invalid conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use points 'infinitely near' to encode tangent/directional conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: If we conceive four points infinitely near respectively to the four former points in the curve (1), the cosines of the direction angles may be expressed as functions of the co-ordinates of the two systems of four points …
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model tangency or directional constraints by introducing 'infinitely near' points (limits) to convert tangent/directional data into positional data that can be used in coefficient-determination arguments.
